title: The Card File and the Curve: Houston, Williamsburg, and the Networks Drawn from the Public Record
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Manlius to Syracuse: The Researcher Before the Artist

stops.name: Manlius, the birth the record gives twice
stops.date_confidence: The year 1951 is institutional (MoMA and Pierogi biographical materials, which give the year and the city of Syracuse only). The exact day, 23 March, and the village of Manlius come from obituary-derived secondary sources (Wikipedia, after Roberta Smith, New York Times, 25 March 2000). The two levels of specificity are held apart here rather than merged into one fact.
stops.campa: A son is born to the Lombardis at Manlius, a village east of Syracuse in the snowbelt of central New York. The institutions that will one day hold his papers record only a year and the nearest city. The newspapers that write him up the week he dies record the day, the twenty-third of March, and the village itself; the finer of the two records arrives forty-nine years late. His birth enters the archive at two resolutions, from two kinds of authority. He will spend his working life insisting that a fact carries the name of the source it came from.
suggested_refs: Roberta Smith, 'Mark Lombardi, 48, an Artist Who Was Inspired by Scandals,' New York Times, 25 March 2000
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mark Lombardi', citing Smith, New York Times, 25 March 2000
MoMA and Pierogi Gallery biographical materials (year only)

stops.name: Syracuse, chief researcher for Teapot Dome to Watergate
stops.date_confidence: The year 1973 and the role of chief researcher are attested (Wikipedia, describing a multimedia collage exhibition). No located source names a venue or a city for the show. The pin is Syracuse University, where he was an enrolled undergraduate that year; it is an inference from his enrollment, not an attested exhibition site. Month and day unknown, set to 01.
stops.campa: An undergraduate is put to work as chief researcher on a multimedia collage running the length of American political scandal, from the oil leases of Teapot Dome in the nineteen-twenties to the burglary and the tapes still unspooling in Washington that spring. The job is entirely archival: naming who paid whom, in what year, out of which company, with a citation under each. He is twenty-two. Nothing in the assignment calls itself art. Where the collage was shown, and in what room, no source records.
suggested_refs: The 1973 exhibition 'Teapot Dome to Watergate', venue unrecorded in any located source

stops.name: Syracuse, the degree in art history
stops.date_confidence: The B.A. in art history from Syracuse University in 1974 is attested (Pierogi Gallery CV; Wikipedia). Month is not given in any source and is set to June for ordering. No matriculation year is attested anywhere; a 1970 start date found in circulating accounts has no source and is treated here as a gap.
stops.campa: He takes a bachelor's degree in art history and goes to Texas. The training is attribution and connoisseurship, the reading of a picture for what its making discloses about the hands and the money behind it. Nothing in the curriculum prepares a young man for merchant banking, and the banking is what he will need. What it does supply is the discipline of the footnote: the picture is not the claim, the source is the claim. The year he first enrolled is in no record anyone has found. He is twenty-three.
suggested_refs: Pierogi Gallery, Mark Lombardi biography and CV, pierogi2000.com

stops.name: Houston, assistant curator under James Harithas
stops.date_confidence: The post of assistant curator at the Contemporary Arts Museum Houston under director James Harithas is attested (Wikipedia) and dated 1975; month unknown, set to January. Coordinates corrected to the museum's actual address at 5216 Montrose Boulevard (29.7264, -95.3915); a figure of 29.7392, -95.391 in circulation lands in residential Montrose, about 1.4 km from the building.
stops.campa: At the Contemporary Arts Museum on Montrose Boulevard he is hired as assistant curator under James Harithas, a director with an appetite for the political and the unsalable. He is twenty-four and a thousand miles from Syracuse. Houston in the middle seventies is an oil town flush with money and thin on institutions, which means the junior curator handles everything, and learns from it what it costs to hang a room and whose money hangs it: checklists, crating, wall labels, the artists themselves.
suggested_refs: Contemporary Arts Museum Houston, 5216 Montrose Boulevard, exhibition records of the Harithas directorship

stops.name: Houston, the reference desk in the Fine Arts department
stops.date_confidence: The post is attested but usually misstated: Wikipedia has him a general reference librarian assigned to the Fine Arts department of the Houston Public Library, not a Fine Arts librarian. No source gives a start year; 1976 is inferred from the close of the museum tenure and is not documented. Address and coordinates corrected: the Julia Ideson Building is 550 McKinney Street (29.7589, -95.3690), not 500, and a figure of 29.7594, -95.3632 falls some 560 m east of it.
stops.campa: He becomes a general reference librarian assigned to the Fine Arts department of the Houston Public Library and builds there, file by file, an archive of the region's artists. The work is the answering of other people's questions with sources: where a fact lives, which index reaches it, whether the name in one document is the same name as in another. Later writers read the librarian as a rehearsal for the artist. That reading is an art historian's inference. He never says it himself in anything that survives.
suggested_refs: The Julia Ideson Building, Houston Public Library, and its regional artist files
sources: OpenStreetMap geocoding of the Julia Ideson Building, 550 McKinney Street

stops.name: Houston, Square One and a gallery under his own name
stops.date_confidence: [R] Reconstruction, and the sources conflict. Square One is named in one source only (Wikipedia), undated; one account implies 1976, another the late 1970s into the 1980s. A Lombardi Gallery appears in general biographical tradition with no institutional sourcing located at all, and Pierogi's own CV mentions neither gallery. No street address survives for either, so the pin is downtown Houston and marks the city, not a gallery site. The 1977 date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He opens a small gallery called Square One, and at some point another carrying his own surname. The Houston alternative-space scene of these years runs on cheap rent and unpaid labour, and galleries in it open and close without leaving deeds behind; neither address can be found in anything reachable, and the years disagree from account to account. Pierogi's later list of his exhibitions mentions neither gallery. For fifteen years he curates, catalogues, sells, hangs and shelves other people's work. He makes none of his own.
suggested_refs: Houston alternative gallery scene of the late 1970s and 1980s; no address recorded for Square One or the Lombardi Gallery
sources: General biographical tradition (Lombardi Gallery, institutional sourcing not located)

stops.name: Houston, the years of abstract painting
stops.date_confidence: [R] Reconstruction. That he worked for years as an abstract, neo-geometric painter before the break is general biographical consensus in MoMA and Pierogi materials, undated. A work of 1984 is cited in retrospective literature as prescient of the later diagrams, but no such work was located in any reachable collection database or gallery CV, and neither his own artist statement nor MoMA's dating includes it in the Narrative Structures, which begin in 1994. No studio address is recorded; the pin is the city.
stops.campa: For most of a decade he paints: abstract, neo-geometric, the flat vocabulary of the period. Retrospective writing likes to point at a canvas of 1984 and call it prescient of the diagrams to come. His own statement does not, and the museum that holds his papers dates the mature series ten years later. That canvas has not been located in any collection record that can be reached. The paintings are not a preparation for anything. They are what he does for a decade, and in the next room the clipping files thicken.
suggested_refs: The 1984 work cited in retrospective literature as a precursor, not located in any reachable collection record
sources: MoMA and Pierogi biographical materials (abstract period, undated)

stops.name: Houston, the scandals in the clipping file
stops.date_confidence: Attested only as 'the early 1990s' (Wikipedia) for research into BCCI and the savings and loan crisis. No source gives a year; 1992 is an ordering device. A date of 1990 in circulation derives from the claimed inclusive range of the MoMA papers, 1990-2000, which is a different thing and not a research start date.
stops.campa: In the early nineties he starts reading the financial scandals the way he once read exhibition histories: the Bank of Credit and Commerce International coming apart in a dozen jurisdictions at once, the savings and loan collapse eating through Texas, Harken Energy and the men around it. The material is entirely public. It is wire copy, court filings, the business pages, the testimony of committees. How thirty parties and four countries are supposed to fit inside a single English sentence is a question none of the coverage answers.
suggested_refs: The BCCI litigation record and the United States savings and loan crisis coverage of 1989-1992, his stated raw material

stops.name: Houston, the tree chart of Khashoggi's holdings
stops.date_confidence: The break from painting to the Narrative Structures is dated 1994 by Lombardi's own artist statement and by MoMA's archive. The Khashoggi anecdote itself is [R]: the quotation circulates in secondary biographical accounts and was not verified here against any primary text. Month unknown, set to January.
stops.campa: Tracking the American holdings of the Saudi arms broker Adnan Khashoggi, he stops writing sentences and draws a tree instead: a name, a line, a company, another line down to the next. It holds. Within days there are more charts, and the abstract painting stops for good, at forty-three, after fifteen years of it. He calls the drawings narrative structures, because each one is a story told as a network. The account of that first chart survives only at second hand; no primary text of it has been produced.
stops.quote: I began taking notes, then sketching out a simple tree chart, showing the breakdown of Khashoggi's American holdings. Within days, I began making more of these charts, depicting other corporate networks I had researched.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Mark Lombardi in secondary biographical accounts; not verified here against a primary source text
suggested_refs: Lombardi's drawings of the Khashoggi holdings, the first of the Narrative Structures
sources: Lombardi, 'The Recent Drawings: An Overview,' Cabinet, issue 2, Spring 2001 (1994 break)
MoMA archival dating of the series
Secondary biographical accounts (the tree chart anecdote, unverified)

stops.name: Houston, the rules of the drawing
stops.date_confidence: The method is his own and is codified in his statement in Cabinet, issue 2, Spring 2001. Dating the rules to 1994 is an ordering device, since the drawings they govern begin that year; the written statement itself is attested only to 2001, and any earlier date for it is inference. Month set to June for ordering.
stops.campa: The system settles into rules. Stacked parallel lines carry a time frame. Radiating arrows carry hierarchy and the direction money moves. Black is the body of the story; red is what a court has said about it, the indictments, the judgments, the sums recovered. Graphite first, because graphite can be revised when the wire copy revises itself. Over all of it stands one rule: nothing enters a drawing that a published source has not already put in public. The rule reaches print only in 2001, a year after his death.
stops.quote: Every statement of fact and connection depicted in the work is true and based on information culled entirely from the public record.
stops.quote_source: Mark Lombardi, 'The Recent Drawings: An Overview,' Cabinet, issue 2, Spring 2001
suggested_refs: Cabinet magazine, issue 2, 'Mapping Conversations,' Spring 2001, cabinetmagazine.org/issues/2/lombardi.php
sources: Mark Lombardi, 'The Recent Drawings: An Overview,' Cabinet, issue 2, Spring 2001

stops.name: Houston, the drawings first on a wall
stops.date_confidence: [R] Reconstruction, and contested. One account states a 1995 Houston debut of the Narrative Structures without naming exhibition or venue; Pierogi's own CV lists no 1995 Houston show and gives the 1996 Lawndale exhibition as the earliest solo. The CV's group-exhibition list does reach back to 1995, so a showing that year is possible but unattested. No venue is named anywhere, so the pin is downtown Houston and marks the city only. Month unknown, set to January.
stops.campa: The first of the diagrams go up somewhere in Houston, in a year the record cannot agree on. One account gives a debut in 1995; the gallery that later represented him lists nothing before the following year. What they look like at this stage is not in doubt: graphite on paper, the arcs drawn with a drafting curve so that an eye can follow a single line across a crowded field without losing it, every node hand-lettered. They hang, and almost nobody looks.
suggested_refs: Pierogi Gallery CV, which lists no 1995 Houston exhibition
sources: MoMA finding aid as reported (1995 Houston debut, venue unnamed)

stops.name: Houston, Over The Line at Lawndale
stops.date_confidence: Run dates attested exactly by Lawndale's own exhibition archive: 23 November 1996 to 18 January 1997. Two corrections to circulating accounts: the venue was then the Lawndale Art and Performance Center, and this was a solo exhibition of his work, not a show he curated. Coordinates corrected to 4912 Main Street (29.7299, -95.3867); a figure of 29.7223, -95.3781 sits about 1.1 km southeast of the building.
stops.campa: Over The Line: Drawings 1994-6 opens at the Lawndale Art and Performance Center on Main Street. It is his first solo exhibition; Pierogi's list of his shows has nothing before it. Two years of work hangs at once, the banking structures and the shell companies together, and a room of them does what a single sheet cannot: it shows the method as a method, repeatable across subjects by anyone willing to do the reading. He is forty-five, newly divorced, and by now packing for New York. The show closes on the eighteenth of January.
suggested_refs: Lawndale Art Center exhibition archive, lawndaleartcenter.org/exhibitions/archive
sources: Pierogi Gallery CV, which lists the show under solo exhibitions

segments.name: Williamsburg and the New York Years

stops.name: Williamsburg, the move north
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia dates the divorce and the move to October 1996; institutional materials give a 1996-97 range, and the range is what is carried here. No street address is recorded in any reachable source, so the pin is the neighbourhood.
stops.campa: Divorced, he leaves Houston for Brooklyn at the urging of the painter Fred Tomaselli and takes a place in Williamsburg, then still a district of cheap lofts and artists who have not yet been priced out of it. He is forty-five and starting again in a city where nobody knows he ever ran a gallery. The drawings travel north rolled in tubes. One account dates the move to October; institutional material gives only a span running into 1997, and no source reachable here records the address.
suggested_refs: Fred Tomaselli's account of urging the move, cited in press coverage of Lombardi

stops.name: Williamsburg, the tape Andy Mann shoots
stops.date_confidence: The video is dated 1996 by Wikipedia, correcting a widely repeated 1997 that appears in most accounts of him. Month and location are not recorded anywhere; because 1996 is also the year of the move, the footage may have been shot in Houston rather than Brooklyn, so the pin is an inference from his base at the end of that year. The quotation is from the Cabinet statement, not from the tape.
stops.campa: The videographer Andy Mann sets a camera in front of him, and for once he explains himself at length: he wants a form with the visual impact of a painting and the informational capacity of a narrative, and he draws his connecting lines as smooth curves so the eye can hold one thread through a hundred crossings without slipping onto another. It is the only substantial interview with him on film. Where the tape was shot nobody records, and 1996 is also the year he leaves Houston.
stops.quote: I call them 'narrative structures' because each consists of a network of lines and notations that are meant to convey a story, typically a recent event of interest to me.
stops.quote_source: Mark Lombardi, 'The Recent Drawings: An Overview,' Cabinet, issue 2, Spring 2001
suggested_refs: Andy Mann's 1996 video interview, screened at Pierogi's 'Index', 2011

stops.name: SoHo, Selections: Winter 1997 at the Drawing Center
stops.date_confidence: The exhibition is attested (Wikipedia lists 'Selections: Winter 1997' at the Drawing Center). The load-bearing half of the usual claim, that MoMA's own archival biography calls this the launch of his wider recognition, could not be verified: moma.org returns HTTP 403 to every request and no Wayback snapshot of the finding aid exists. Month unknown, set to January.
stops.campa: The Drawing Center on Wooster Street puts him into its winter Selections, the open-submission show New York uses to find out who has arrived. His sheets hang among draughtsmen doing figures and landscapes, and they are read first as drawings, which is what he wants, before anyone reads them as arguments. What got him through the submissions is the graphite and the drafting curve, not the banks. He is forty-five and has been showing other people's work for two decades. Whether the museum that holds his papers calls this the start of his recognition cannot be checked; its finding aid is unreachable.
suggested_refs: The Drawing Center, 35 Wooster Street, 'Selections: Winter 1997'

stops.name: Turin, Versus IV
stops.date_confidence: [R] Reconstruction. The inclusion in the group exhibition 'Versus IV' at Turin in 1998 is listed in his exhibition record (Wikipedia); the host institution is not confirmed in any located source, and the pin is the city of Turin rather than a venue. Month unknown, set to January.
stops.campa: The work crosses to Italy for a group show called Versus IV. The show is listed in his exhibition record and nowhere else; which room in Turin held the sheets is not recorded in anything that can be reached, and the city's own banking history is not among his subjects. The diagrams travel without him and without translation. A viewer with no English can still follow an arc from a name to a bank to a date, which is the argument for making the thing a picture at all. He does not go.
suggested_refs: 'Versus IV', Turin, 1998, host institution unrecorded in located sources

stops.name: Washington, Crossing the Line
stops.date_confidence: [R] Reconstruction. Pierogi's own CV gives 'Crossing the Line, MoCA Washington, D.C.' in 1998, a small Georgetown contemporary-art space; the title suffix '1994-8' and a gloss connecting the show to the Hirshhorn appear in circulating accounts, are unsupported by any located source, and are not repeated here. No address for MOCA DC was found, so the pin is the Washington city centroid and marks the city only. Month unknown, set to June for ordering.
stops.campa: A show called Crossing the Line carries the drawings to Washington, to a small contemporary space in Georgetown rather than to any museum on the Mall. The city on the walls is the city outside them: First American Bankshares, the committee rooms, the sworn testimony. Whether anyone from those rooms walked in is not recorded. Pierogi's own list gives the venue as MoCA Washington and nothing further. Neither the street address nor the run of the show survives in any source now reachable.
suggested_refs: Pierogi Gallery CV, '1998 Crossing the Line, MoCA Washington, D.C.'
sources: Retrospective literature (venue named only as MCA/MoCA Washington)

stops.name: Williamsburg, Silent Partners at Pierogi
stops.date_confidence: November 1998 at Pierogi 2000 is attested twice over (Wikipedia; Pierogi's own CV). The New York Times 'Art in Review' notice of 25 December 1998 cited in secondary accounts could not be verified here: nytimes.com is not fetchable from this machine. Day unknown, set to 01.
stops.campa: Silent Partners opens at Pierogi, ten minutes' walk from his apartment, and it is the show that makes him a New York artist instead of a Houston one. The gallery has wall enough to hang the long sheets at full length, and at full length the drawings stop looking like charts and start looking like weather systems. A notice in the Times before the year is out is cited in every later account of him, always at second hand. The notice itself could not be produced here.
stops.quote: One of my goals is to explore the interaction of political, social, and economic forces in contemporary affairs.
stops.quote_source: Mark Lombardi, 'The Recent Drawings: An Overview,' Cabinet, issue 2, Spring 2001
suggested_refs: Pierogi 2000, 177 North 9th Street, Brooklyn, 'Silent Partners', November 1998

stops.name: Chelsea, Vicious Circles
stops.date_confidence: The exhibition is attested by Pierogi's CV as 'Vicious Circles: Drawings, Deven Golden Fine Art, New York', 1999, which also settles the spelling: 'Devon Golden Gallery' found elsewhere is the error. The attribution of the phrase 'poetry of paranoia' to a Ken Johnson review in the New York Times could not be verified, nytimes.com being unfetchable here, and is carried as unverified. The pin is a generic Chelsea point; the gallery's street address was not located. Month unknown, set to January.
stops.campa: Vicious Circles: Drawings opens at Deven Golden Fine Art in Chelsea, and the vocabulary that follows him for the rest of his life and long past it attaches here: paranoia, conspiracy, the poetry of both. He objects to the words every time he is handed them. The drawings contain no secret and posit no hidden hand; they contain what has already been printed, arranged so its shape can be taken in at a glance. Who first wrote the poetry of paranoia about him is a question the sources here cannot settle.
suggested_refs: Ken Johnson's New York Times review of 'Vicious Circles', source of the phrase 'poetry of paranoia' (attribution unverified)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mark Lombardi' (with the gallery name misspelled)

stops.name: Williamsburg, the Bank of Credit and Commerce International
stops.date_confidence: The BCCI series is attested and ten of its drawings are in the Whitney Museum's collection. The date is an ordering device: the series was revised across years and no source gives a date for individual versions beyond the inclusive 1996-2000 of the fourth. That Clark Clifford appears as a node rests on art-historical accounts of the work rather than on a reproduction examined here, and is [R] at that level of detail.
stops.campa: He draws the bank Agha Hasan Abedi founded in 1972, chartered in Luxembourg, run out of Leadenhall Street until it came apart in 1991 across a dozen jurisdictions: the deposits, the nominees, the auditors who signed. The structure is the whole point. Clark Clifford chairs First American Bankshares in Washington while the bank owns it through men holding shares on behalf of other men, and that arrangement cannot be put in a sentence without dissolving. Drawn, it is one shape.
stops.quote: Working from syndicated news items and other published accounts, I begin each drawing by compiling large amounts of information about a specific bank, financial group, or set of individuals.
stops.quote_source: Mark Lombardi, 'The Recent Drawings: An Overview,' Cabinet, issue 2, Spring 2001
suggested_refs: The ten BCCI/ICIC/FAB drawings in the collection of the Whitney Museum of American Art
The Kerry Committee report on BCCI, United States Senate, 1992
sources: Whitney Museum collection record as cited in the research brief
Art-historical accounts of the BCCI series (nodes named)

stops.name: Williamsburg, Lake Resources and the arms pipeline
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a subject of the Narrative Structures: the drawing pairing Oliver North, Lake Resources of Panama and the Iran-Contra operation. That William Casey and Manuel Noriega appear as nodes within the same structure rests on art-historical accounts of the work rather than on any reproduction examined here, and is [R]. The date orders the segment; no date for the individual sheet was located.
stops.campa: Another sheet takes the money out of the Iran arms sales into a Credit Suisse account in Geneva called Lake Resources and back out again to the airstrip at Ilopango. Oliver North signs for it. William Casey at Langley backs the channel. Manuel Noriega banks along Calle 50 in Panama City with the same institution the BCCI sheet describes, so the two drawings share a node. None of it is secret. All of it was said under oath in Washington in 1987 and printed the next morning.
stops.quote: Certain things that are listed in the drawing are in red. These represent court judgments, actual dollar amounts. That is verifiable information.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Mark Lombardi in secondary accounts of his method; not verified here against a primary source text
suggested_refs: Report of the Congressional Committees Investigating the Iran-Contra Affair, 1987, the published record beneath the drawing
sources: Art-historical accounts of the Iran-Contra structure (nodes named)

stops.name: Williamsburg, Harken Energy and the World Finance Corporation
stops.date_confidence: Ordering device. The Harken cluster (George W. Bush, Harken Energy and Jackson Stephens) and the World Finance Corporation, Miami drawings are attested as Lombardi subjects; no date for the individual sheets was located, and the Harken connection is [R] at the level of which figures appear on which version.
stops.campa: One drawing follows George W. Bush, then a Texas oilman with a failing company, through Harken Energy and the Arkansas financier Jackson Stephens. Another maps the World Finance Corporation of Miami, whose directory of Cuban exiles and narcotics prosecutions the federal record had already written down at length. Both subjects were public property before he touched them, and he accuses nobody of anything. Which figures stand on which version of the Harken sheet is not settled by any reproduction examined here.
suggested_refs: Lombardi's 'World Finance Corporation, Miami' group and the Harken Energy drawings
sources: QUEUE.md entry for Mark Lombardi (subject clusters)

stops.name: Williamsburg, the index cards
stops.date_confidence: The card archive is attested; its extent is contradicted between sources and the contradiction is not resolved here. Contemporary exhibition materials give roughly 14,500 cards, the only figure independently corroborated. MoMA's processed finding aid is reported to describe over 10,000 cards in sixteen boxes across sixteen linear feet, dated 1990-2000 and colour-coded pink for companies and green for people, but moma.org returns HTTP 403 to every request and archive.org holds no snapshot of the finding aid, so that description is uncorroborated. Date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Behind every sheet stands a card file: three inches by five, hand-written, one fact and one citation to a card, pink for a company and green for a person. He lays them out on a table and shuffles them into sequence until the sequence makes a shape, and only then is the shape drawn. How many cards there are is a question the sources answer differently, fourteen and a half thousand by one count, something over ten thousand by another. Nobody has reconciled the two numbers.
stops.quote: My purpose throughout is to interpret the material by juxtaposing and assembling the notations into a unified, coherent whole.
stops.quote_source: Mark Lombardi, 'The Recent Drawings: An Overview,' Cabinet, issue 2, Spring 2001
suggested_refs: The Mark Lombardi Papers, Museum of Modern Art Archives, New York
sources: MoMA processed finding aid as reported (10,000+, 16 boxes, 16 linear feet), uncorroborated

stops.name: Williamsburg, the fourth version
stops.date_confidence: The work is dated 1996-2000 and is one of ten Lombardi drawings in the Whitney Museum's collection; the ten-work holding is attested. Its reported width of roughly 11.5 feet could not be verified, whitney.org returning 404 to every path tried, and is not asserted here. The pin is his Brooklyn studio, where the sheet was made, not the museum that later held it. Month unknown, set to January.
stops.campa: BCCI-ICIC & FAB, 1972-91, fourth version, is finished after four years of revision, a single sheet wider than most rooms. It is not a reprint of the three before it. Each version absorbs whatever the litigation has disclosed since the last one, so the drawing grows the way a case grows, and the date written on it is a span of years rather than a day. On the seventeenth of October 2001, eighteen months after his death, an agent of the FBI telephones the museum that owns it and asks to be let in front of it. How wide the sheet actually is, that museum's own record would say. It cannot be reached.
stops.quote: Black represents the essential elements of the story while major lawsuits, criminal indictments, or other legal actions taken against the parties are illustrated with red.
stops.quote_source: Mark Lombardi, 'The Recent Drawings: An Overview,' Cabinet, issue 2, Spring 2001
suggested_refs: Robert Hobbs on the FBI's request of 17 October 2001 to see the drawing at the Whitney: 'she unwittingly made history'

stops.name: Long Island City, Greater New York
stops.date_confidence: Only 'February 2000' is attested (Wikipedia). The day-precise opening of 27 February found in circulating accounts could not be corroborated: moma.org and MoMA PS1 pages return HTTP 403 and no encyclopedia article for the exhibition exists. Day set to 01 accordingly. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap.
stops.campa: P.S.1 in Long Island City opens Greater New York: New Art in New York Now, a survey of who is working in the city at this moment, and he is in it at forty-eight after twenty-five years of hanging other people's shows. It is the largest audience the drawings have ever had. Friends who see him that month describe a man strained about money and about the work. The month is all that is attested; the opening day of the twenty-seventh, repeated everywhere, is corroborated nowhere.
suggested_refs: 'Greater New York: New Art in New York Now', P.S.1 Contemporary Art Center, February 2000

stops.name: Long Island City, water on the paper
stops.date_confidence: [R] Reconstruction, weakly sourced, and the accounts contradict each other on place. A sprinkler malfunction damaging a BCCI drawing before Greater New York is repeated in material about this period, but no source for it was located anywhere: not in the encyclopedia article, not in Pierogi's CV, not in any reachable exhibition record. One account places the incident at P.S.1, another at an unspecified Manhattan site. The date is an ordering device. Deliberate sabotage is asserted by no source with evidence and is not asserted here.
stops.campa: A sprinkler head lets go and water comes down on one of the BCCI drawings. Graphite on paper takes water badly, and he sets about repairing it in the weeks before the opening. The story is retold afterwards with a knowing inflection, because a damaged BCCI drawing shortly before a suspicious death makes a better story than a leak does. The duller version is the one the evidence supports, and the evidence for even the duller version has not been produced.
suggested_refs: Press and exhibition accounts of damage to a BCCI drawing before 'Greater New York', 2000, primary source not located
sources: Institutional and press accounts referenced in the research brief, no primary source located

stops.name: Williamsburg, the apartment
stops.date_confidence: Attested. MoMA's archival finding aid, the record of the institution that holds his papers, states that the death was suicide by hanging; corroborated by Roberta Smith's obituary, New York Times, 25 March 2000, and Adrian Dannatt's, The Independent, 16 May 2000. The murder rumours amplified by Patricia Goldstone's Interlock (2015) are recorded as rumour: no located evidence overturns the institutional finding. No street address appears in any reachable source, so the pin is the neighbourhood.
stops.campa: He dies in his Williamsburg apartment on the twenty-second of March, the day before his forty-ninth birthday, having shortly before moved his work out of it and into the gallery. The finding is suicide by hanging and the museum that holds his papers states it without hedging. Fifteen years later a biography will reopen the question, and a certain kind of reader has not closed it since, on the reasoning that a man who drew arms dealers cannot have died of himself. He was forty-eight, in debt, and five weeks out from the largest show of his life.
suggested_refs: Patricia Goldstone, Interlock: Art, Conspiracy, and the Shadow Worlds of Mark Lombardi (2015), the principal carrier of the murder rumour

stops.name: Williamsburg, the statement printed a year late
stops.date_confidence: The statement appeared in Cabinet, issue 2, 'Mapping Conversations,' Spring 2001, a year after his death; its composition date is unknown. Month set to March for ordering. The pin is his own Brooklyn base, where the text was written; Cabinet's office address is not on record and the magazine itself is not pinned here.
stops.campa: The Recent Drawings: An Overview appears in the second issue of Cabinet, a year after he is dead. It runs a few hundred words, and it is the only place in which he sets out the whole system in his own hand and under his own name: what the parallel lines do, what the arrows do, why black and why red, and the standard that governs all of it. Every argument made about him afterwards is made against this page, by the people who quote it and by the people who prefer not to.
stops.quote: In some cases I use a set of stacked, parallel lines to establish a time frame. Hierarchical relationships, the flow of money, and other key details are then indicated by a system of radiating arrows, broken lines, and so forth.
stops.quote_source: Mark Lombardi, 'The Recent Drawings: An Overview,' Cabinet, issue 2, Spring 2001

stops.name: Ithaca, Global Networks opens
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Independent Curators International's own record: Herbert F. Johnson Museum of Art, Cornell University, 25 January to 16 March 2003, the first venue of the tour Robert Hobbs curated. The tour ran to 2005, not 2003 as often stated. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap.
stops.campa: Three years after his death the Herbert F. Johnson Museum at Cornell opens Mark Lombardi: Global Networks, the survey Robert Hobbs assembled for Independent Curators International. From Ithaca it travels to Cleveland, to Ann Arbor, to the Drawing Center, to San Francisco, to Syracuse where he took his degree, to Grinnell, and closes at Milwaukee in the April of 2005. Two full years on the road for a body of work made by one man at a table with a card file.

stops.name: SoHo, the tour comes back to Wooster Street
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Independent Curators International's tour record, which gives the Drawing Center as a venue from 1 November 2003; no closing date is given there. This is the same institution whose 'Selections: Winter 1997' first brought the work to New York attention.
stops.campa: The travelling retrospective reaches the Drawing Center, six years after the same building took three sheets into an open-submission group show and let New York find him. The drawings hang now with wall texts explaining who Agha Hasan Abedi was and what Lake Resources of Panama did, which is a service the sheets were built not to need, since every name on them is lettered with its own line running out to whatever else it touched. The rooms are full every day of the run. Downstairs, the submissions for the next Selections come in from artists nobody has yet heard of.

stops.name: San Francisco, UPI Saga
stops.date_confidence: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art's acquisition of 'UPI Saga' in 2004 is taken from its collection record as cited in the research brief and was not independently confirmed here. Month unknown, set to January.
stops.campa: SFMOMA buys UPI Saga, which follows the ownership of United Press International from investor to investor as the wire service is handed along like a debt that nobody wants to be holding. It is one of the single-subject sheets, narrower in reach than the banking structures and easier to take in at one standing, and it enters a museum collection on the far coast from any event it describes. Four years after the funeral, the institutions that ignored him alive begin, methodically, to buy.

stops.name: Midtown, sixteen boxes at the Museum of Modern Art
stops.date_confidence: The Museum of Modern Art holds the Lombardi papers. The reported detail of the donation, that his father Donald Lombardi gave the archive through Pierogi Gallery in 2006, and the finding aid's extent of sixteen boxes and sixteen linear feet, could not be corroborated: moma.org returns HTTP 403 to every request and archive.org holds no snapshot of the finding aid. Month unknown, set to January.
stops.campa: His father gives the card file to the Museum of Modern Art through the gallery that showed him, and a museum built to collect finished objects takes in a working method instead: boxes of three-by-five cards, each carrying one fact with the place it came from written underneath. What is catalogued is not the drawings but the evidence standing behind the drawings. A researcher can now check him card by card, which is precisely the test he asked to be given.

stops.name: Madrid, the Reina Sofia acquisition
stops.date_confidence: [R] Reconstruction. That the Museo Reina Sofia holds Lombardi is attested by Pierogi's own list of collections. The identification of the work as the Nugan Hand Ltd, Sydney drawing and the acquisition year 2008 are unverified: every museoreinasofia.es collection path tried returned 404 and the site search surfaced nothing for him. Month unknown, set to January. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap.
stops.campa: A Lombardi enters the Reina Sofia in Madrid, reportedly the sheet on Nugan Hand Ltd, the Sydney merchant bank whose collapse in 1980 spilled retired American officers, arms shipments and a dead founder across the Australian press of the early eighties. A bank in Sydney, drawn in Houston or Brooklyn out of newspaper cuttings, hanging now off the Paseo del Prado: the network the drawings describe is transnational and so, by degrees, is their afterlife. Which drawing it is, and in what year it was bought, are claims this record cannot confirm. That the museum holds him is not in doubt.

stops.name: Kassel, the Fridericianum
stops.date_confidence: His inclusion in dOCUMENTA (13) is confirmed on documenta.de's own artist list. The commonly repeated identification of his contribution with the notebook '100 Notes - 100 Thoughts No. 071' is not confirmed anywhere: documenta.de does not connect him to the series and Hatje Cantz, its publisher, returns no result for the pairing, so the notebook number is dropped here. Month and day unknown, set to 01. Coordinates corrected to the Fridericianum's actual position; two different wrong pins for the same building are in circulation.
stops.campa: Twelve years dead, he is shown at dOCUMENTA in Kassel, the exhibition that decides every five years what contemporary art is currently for. In the same year five computer scientists publish a paper defining a Lombardi drawing as a formal class of graph layout: every edge a perfectly circular arc, and perfect angular resolution at every vertex. His name passes into mathematics as a specification. It is a stranger afterlife than the museums, and a more exact one.

stops.name: Midtown, the film at the museum that holds his papers
stops.date_confidence: Mareike Wegener's documentary premiered in Germany at the end of May 2012 and screened at the Brooklyn Film Festival that spring, reaching MoMA that September (Wikipedia, citing ArtInfo, the Huffington Post and the New York Times; Wikidata gives the premiere as 31 May 2012). A 2011 date appearing in some accounts is wrong. Day unknown, set to 01.
stops.campa: Mareike Wegener's Death-Defying Acts of Art and Conspiracy reaches the museum that holds his papers, after Germany at the end of May and the Brooklyn Film Festival in the spring. The film refuses both of the available endings. It will not make him a seer who decoded the world in graphite, and it will not make him a man killed for knowing too much. What is left standing when both endings are refused is a librarian who worked extremely hard and died at forty-eight.

stops.name: Madison Avenue, Everything Is Connected
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the exhibition ran at The Met Breuer, 945 Madison Avenue, 18 September 2018 to 6 January 2019 (Pierogi's own announcement). Accounts placing it in the Metropolitan Museum's Fifth Avenue building are wrong by some seven hundred metres; the coordinates here are the Breuer building's, from OpenStreetMap.
stops.campa: The Metropolitan hangs him in its Breuer building, in a show called Everything Is Connected: Art and Conspiracy, beside Hans Haacke, Jenny Holzer, Mike Kelley and Trevor Paglen. Haacke is the precedent every writer reaches for, the artist who made a work out of a Manhattan landlord's public property filings and had a Guggenheim show cancelled over it. The title is the sentence Lombardi spent his life being accused of believing, printed above work that only ever repeated what a court had already said.
